question: Before anyone presses an oil, what do people cook, burn and anoint with — and where do the first oil crops come from?
summary: For most of this folio fat is *animal* fat. The oldest way to get it is rendering, heating tissue until the fat separates ([[te1]]); the first dairy fat, butter, arrives with Neolithic herders milking sheep and goats ([[ec1]]); and by about 1600 BC the oldest known recipes, the Babylonian cooking tablets, start almost every dish with water and then fat ([[e1]]). In hot Mesopotamia butter is always clarified so that it keeps, the ancestor of ghee ([[ec6]]). Which fat a region uses depends on its climate and pasture before it depends on anything else ([[w1]]).

The oil crops appear in the same long span, and their record is mostly botanical. The olive is domesticated in the Chalcolithic Levant ([[ec2]]), flax serves for oil and fibre ([[ec3]]), sesame is grown at Harappa and carried to Mesopotamia and Egypt ([[ec4]], [[x1]], [[x2]]), and by the Late Bronze Age Crete, Cyprus and the palace economies of the Levant press and store olive oil on a large scale ([[te2]], [[ec8]], [[ec9]]). Far away, sunflower and soybean are domesticated on different continents with no contact between them ([[ec13]], [[ec14]]). Africa and the Americas enter at the margins: herders in the green Sahara heat milk in pots in the fifth millennium BC ([[ec10]]); oil-palm shells turn up at African sites from about 3000 BC on one unverified abstract ([[ec11]]); and peanuts are grown in Peru by 2000 BC ([[ec12]]). Egypt’s own best oil, nhh, is a name nobody can identify ([[th2]]). The north’s fat includes the sea: Baltic hunter-gatherers burn blubber lamps and keep cooking marine and freshwater food in their pots when farming arrives ([[te4]], [[ec15]]). The older story — bone grease, fat lamps and the first pots — is the folio before this one.

The folio's point is that fats and oils start as separate stories — herders' fat in the north and east, plant oil in the Mediterranean and the Indus — and that the evidence for the second is much firmer than for the first. Everything later in the program is the movement and substitution of these fats.

themes.title: The fat of animals and milk
text: Rendered tallow and sheep's tail fat, then butter and clarified butter: the herder's fats, and the ones the Babylonian cooks use. The evidence is textual and popular-historical, since the residue studies are not in the library.

themes.title: The olive, from tree to press
text: Charred stones show the tree under cultivation by about 4800–3800 BC; the first evidence of large-scale processing is Late Bronze Age Crete and Cyprus, with palace oil stores reported at Ebla, Mari and Ugarit. Stones and wood date the tree, not the oil.

themes.title: Sesame, the oil crop that travels
text: Sesame is grown at Harappa by about 2600 BC, reaches Mesopotamia by about 2000 BC with its names, is named as an 'oil-plant' in cuneiform from about 2400 BC, and is among Tutankhamun's grave goods. Its identification in the cuneiform is still argued.

themes.title: Other oils, and a doubtful soap
text: Flax for oil and fibre, mustard and linseed in the Indus, palm fat in an Egyptian tomb, and the independent domestication of sunflower and soybean; and a popular claim that soap was made in Babylonia by about 2500 BC, which no source in the library supports.

themes.title: Africa and the Americas: the fats the Mediterranean story leaves out
text: Dairy fat in Saharan pots, the African oil palm, and the New World’s peanut and sunflower. The African entries rest on thin tiers (an abstract, a 1897 analysis), but they show that the oil palm and herders’ milk fat are older than any written record of them.

themes.title: Marine fats of the north
text: Blubber lamps and marine food in Baltic pots show sea fat in use beside the farmers’ animal fat; the blubber-lamp entry rests on a title alone.

turning_points.text: Neolithic herders make the first butter.
The olive is domesticated in the Chalcolithic Levant.
Saharan herders process milk fat in pots.
Sesame is a crop of the Harappan Indus.
Sesame travels to Mesopotamia, with its name.
The Yale culinary tablets put fat in every pot.
Cyprus and Crete press olives at scale.

how_to_read: Start with *Economy* and *Exchange*, where the crops are, then *Technology* for the presses and for rendering. The fat groups run through the folio (Olive Oil, Oilseeds, Butter & Ghee, Palm & Coconut), so a reader can follow one substance across periods.
Most lanes are empty by design: there is almost no evidence for law, belief or conflict about fats before 1200 BC. The next folio is where the olive and sesame get states, gods and laws.

The *picture by region* below shows the balance plainly: more than half the entries are Near Eastern, and Africa and the Americas have only a few between them. That reflects what the library and the botanical record hold, not the history of fats.

sources.intro: Prehistory is a story of plants and pots, so the folio leans on botanical syntheses, specialist volumes on sesame, and a translation of the Babylonian cooking tablets, with popular histories filling the gaps on butter and olive oil.
main: Zohary, Hopf & Weiss, *Domestication of Plants in the Old World*, for the olive and flax ([[ec2]], [[ec3]]).
Bedigian (ed.), *Sesame: The Genus Sesamum*, with Kiple's chapter and Achaya, for sesame ([[ec4]], [[x1]], [[x2]], [[th1]]).
Bottéro, *The Oldest Cuisine in the World*, for the Babylonian recipes and butter ([[e1]], [[ec6]]).
Foxhall, Kiple, Mueller and Khosrova for the olive's Bronze Age and for butter ([[te2]], [[ec8]], [[ec1]]).
Dunne et al. (through a search abstract) and Kiple for Saharan dairying and the peanut ([[ec10]], [[ec12]]); Lynn and one unverified abstract for the African oil palm ([[ec11]]).
contested: The Akkadian 'oil-plant' as sesame rather than flax ([[th1]]); older statements that no sesame came from Mesopotamia are corrected by later finds ([[x1]]).
Palm fat at Abydos rests on one analysis of 1897 ([[ec7]]).
Palace oil stores at Ebla, Mari and Ugarit come from a journalist's summary ([[ec9]]).
The soybean's Chinese dating ([[ec14]]) and the Babylonian soap claim ([[te3]]) are unsettled.
Saharan dairy fat rests on an abstract and press coverage, not the paper ([[ec10]]); the oil-palm shells on one abstract ([[ec11]]); the identity of nhh is argued ([[th2]]).
The blubber lamps are known here only by an article title and context ([[te4]]); the Baltic lipid study only by its abstract ([[ec15]]).
gaps: The lipid-residue studies of Neolithic pottery (Evershed and others), which are the real evidence for early dairying, are not in the library.

Egypt’s oils are now partly covered ([[ec7]], [[x2]], [[th2]]) but not castor, moringa or ben oil; African fats other than the palm and Saharan milk (shea, Ethiopian oilseeds), Chinese oils before 1200 BC, and all of Oceania are missing.
Marine fats beyond the Baltic and Japan — the Arctic, the Pacific coasts, the Indian Ocean fish-eaters — are not covered, and the Near East’s sea fats are missing.

text: Europe enters only through the island palaces of Crete and Cyprus: Crete grows rich on exported oil and the two islands press olives at scale ([[ec8]], [[te2]]). The north’s animal-fat world is described in the climate baseline ([[w1]]), but nothing in the library dates a northern European fat practice before 1200 BC. The sea fat of the Baltic is here too: marine and freshwater food in pots and the blubber lamps of the Late Mesolithic ([[ec15]], [[te4]]).

The core of the folio, because the evidence is here: the first butter and clarified butter, the Chalcolithic olive, flax, palace oil stores, the Babylonian recipes and the inspectors of Ebla ([[ec1]], [[ec2]], [[ec3]], [[ec9]], [[e1]], [[o1]]). Egypt is filed under the Near East in the atlas, though it is African: the palm fat at Abydos, Tutankhamun’s sesame and the argument over nhh ([[ec7]], [[x2]], [[th2]]), and Canaanite oil on the sea routes to Egypt ([[x4]]).

The Harappan Indus: sesame, mustard and linseed, with animal fats beside them ([[ec4]], [[ec5]]), and sesame’s journey west ([[x1]]). China’s one entry is the soybean, whose domestication date (2700 or 1000 BC) is argued in [[ec14]].

Two entries, both at the thin end of the evidence: dairy fat in Saharan pots ([[ec10]]) and oil-palm shells at West and Central African sites ([[ec11]]). Egypt’s entries sit under the Near East. Nothing in the library covers shea, Ethiopian oilseeds or the Nile above Egypt in this period.
Two entries: peanuts grown in Peru by 2000 BC, with Kiple’s note that the New World had few fat animals ([[ec12]]). The sunflower’s domestication in eastern North America is the second ([[ec13]]).
No entry. Nothing in the library dates Pacific fats before 1200 BC; the coconut’s spread across the Pacific is a later folio (fats-300bc-600ad).
The climate baseline that sets the fat by the land ([[w1]]).
